name: Roman Empire
story: The SPQR vexillum flew over a republic turned empire that ruled the Mediterranean for five centuries. Rome rose from a city of seven hills through legions, law and roads, swallowing Carthage, Greece and Gaul, until Goths and Vandals broke through the borders and Odoacer deposed the last emperor in 476.
quizFact: SPQR stands for 'The Senate and People of Rome', and it is still painted on Roman manhole covers today.

name: Byzantine Empire
story: The tetragrammatic cross of the Palaiologos flew over the eastern Rome that outlived the west by a thousand years. Justinian rebuilt the world with Hagia Sophia and his reconquest of Italy and Africa; Heraclius defeated Persia in history's last ancient superpower war - then lost the Levant to the Arab armies within a decade. Betrayal was the empire's chronic disease: Basil I murdered his way to the throne, the Varangian guards changed masters, and in 1204 the Fourth Crusade - sold a bill of goods by Venice - sacked Constantinople itself. The end came on 29 May 1453, when 21-year-old Mehmed II's cannon broke the Theodosian Walls and Emperor Constantine XI died in the breach, his body never identified.
quizFact: Byzantine fire ships used 'Greek fire', a burning liquid that kept burning on water, and its recipe remains a mystery.

name: Ottoman Empire
story: The star and crescent flew over six centuries of conquest: Osman's frontier beylik grew into the empire of Mehmed the Conqueror, who took Constantinople in 1453 at age 21, and Suleiman the Magnificent, whose armies besieged Vienna in 1529. The sultans ran three continents through the devshirme - Christian boys taken as tribute, trained into the empire's fiercest soldiers - and law codified by Suleiman himself. Its fall was a 300-year fade: failed sieges, lost naval wars at Lepanto, nationalist revolts in the Balkans, and finally WWI, after which the Allies partitioned the heartlands and Ataturk abolished the sultanate in 1922, sending the last caliph onto the Orient Express.
quizFact: The same star and crescent still flies over modern Turkey, borrowed straight from the sultans.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
story: Cyrus the Great's standard of a golden falcon-wind god flew over the first true world empire, from Greece to India. It fell when Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BC after three crushing victories.
quizFact: The Cyrus Cylinder, buried under Babylon's walls, is often called the world's first human rights charter.

name: Rashidun Caliphate
story: The plain black banner of the first four caliphs led the Arab armies out of Arabia into Byzantine and Persian lands within a generation. It ended when Ali was assassinated in 661 and the Umayyads took power.
quizFact: In under 30 years this state conquered more territory than Rome had in three centuries.

name: Umayyad Caliphate
story: The white banner of Damascus ruled the largest empire the world had yet seen, from the Atlantic to the Indus. Revolution from the east destroyed the dynasty in 750, though a survivor fled to Spain and kept a rival caliphate alive in Córdoba.
quizFact: Spain was ruled by this dynasty's descendants for almost 300 more years after it fell everywhere else.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
story: The black banners of the Abbasids founded Baghdad's House of Wisdom, where algebra and astronomy flourished. The caliphate faded into figurehead status until the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 and ended it in ink and blood.
quizFact: The Tigris river reportedly ran black with ink from the books thrown into it when the Mongols burned Baghdad.

name: Mughal Empire
story: The green standards of the Timurid dynasty ruled a quarter of humanity at their peak. Babur won an empire with 12,000 men and gunpowder; Akbar ran it with tolerance and a revenue system so fair its paperwork outlived the state; Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for a wife who died delivering their fourteenth child. Aurangzeb's 49-year war against the Marathas emptied the treasury his ancestors filled, and Nadir Shah's 1739 sack of Delhi carried off the Peacock Throne and 700 million rupees. The last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar - a poet who commanded nothing - was tried for the 1857 rebellion and exiled to Rangoon; his sons were shot by a young British captain named Hodson.
quizFact: The Peacock Throne, covered in rubies and emeralds, was valued at more than the rest of the empire's annual revenue.

name: Maratha Empire
story: The saffron Bhagwa flag rose with Shivaji's guerrilla armies against the Mughals and came to rule most of India by 1760. The British broke their confederacy in the three Anglo-Maratha Wars, finishing in 1818.
quizFact: The saffron flag of Shivaji is still a potent symbol in Indian politics three centuries later.

name: British Empire
story: The Union Jack flew over 35.5 million square kilometres - the largest empire in history, governing a quarter of humanity with barely 5,000 British administrators in India. It was built by companies before Parliament: the East India Company kept its own 200,000-man army, and after the 1857 rebellion Britain crowned Victoria Empress. Its ledger holds the Bengal famine of 1943 (three million dead), the Amritsar massacre, the Boer concentration camps, and the slave trade it both ran and eventually hunted down. Two world wars bankrupted it; India's 1947 partition killed a million more in its death throes, and Hong Kong's handover in 1997 closed the ledger.
quizFact: At its peak, there was always at least one territory of this empire in daylight, hence 'the empire on which the sun never sets'.

name: British East India Company
file: Flag of the British East India Company (1801).svg
story: A company with its own army ruled Bengal after Plassey (1757) and swallowed most of India behind the striped ensign. The horrific 1857 rebellion made London abolish company rule and crown Victoria Empress of India.
quizFact: The company's striped flag inspired the flag of the United States, which adopted stripes just after the company's ensign became famous.

name: Spanish Empire (Cross of Burgundy)
story: The saltire of Burgundy flew over Spain's Golden Century: Cortes toppled the Aztecs with 600 men and a million indigenous allies, Pizarro strangled the Inca state after collecting a room of gold for Atahualpa's life and killing him anyway, and Manila galleons carried American silver to Asia. Potosi's mountain alone yielded 45,000 tonnes of silver, much of it mined by the mita labor draft that worked men to death underground. The empire's ruin was written in its ledgers: five state bankruptcies in a century, the Armada's destruction in 1588, and Napoleon's 1808 invasion that triggered the American wars of liberation under Bolivar and San Martin.
quizFact: This flag still flies over a few forts in the Caribbean and is used by a modern Flemish nationalist movement.

name: Dutch East India Company (VOC)
file: Flag of the Dutch East India Company.svg
story: The tricolour with the VOC monogram flew over the richest company in history, running the spice trade from Batavia and founding Cape Town and New Amsterdam. Corruption and war with Britain bankrupted it; its lands became the Dutch East Indies, then Indonesia.
quizFact: The VOC was worth more than Apple, Google and Amazon combined at today's prices, and paid 18% yearly returns for two centuries.

name: Kingdom of France
story: The fleur-de-lis banner carried France from the fields of Crecy to the banks of the Mississippi. It was the flag of Joan of Arc's relieving armies, of Louis XIV's Versailles - where 10,000 nobles were tamed into courtiers - and of the fur traders who claimed half of North America. Its end was swift and self-inflicted: bankrupt from the Seven Years' War and the American Revolution it funded, the crown called the Estates General in 1789, lost control of the revolution it summoned, and Louis XVI went to the guillotine in January 1793 before a crowd that had once shouted for his grandfather.
quizFact: White was France's royal color for 500 years; revolutionaries swapped it for the red and blue of Paris.

name: Napoleonic France
story: The tricolour rode with the largest armies Europe had ever seen - 600,000 men crossed into Russia in 1812, and fewer than 100,000 came home. Napoleon rose from a minor Corsican family to crown himself emperor at 34, beating Austrians, Russians and Prussians in single campaigns; he sold Louisiana to pay for war, reinstated colonial slavery he had once abolished, and shot his way through Spain. His downfall was arithmetic: Britain's money, Russia's winter, and every power he had humiliated returning together in 1813-15. Waterloo ended it, but his Code still governs courts on five continents.
quizFact: Napoleon's soldiers digging fortifications in Egypt found the Rosetta Stone, unlocking hieroglyphs.

name: Kingdom of Prussia
story: The black and white banner of a disciplined kingdom that rose from a sandpit of Brandenburg to unify Germany. Bismarck engineered victory over France in 1871 and proclaimed the German Empire in Versailles' Hall of Mirrors; the Prussian state was formally abolished by the Allies in 1947.
quizFact: Prussia's army drill discipline was so famous that 'Prussian' became a synonym for rigid precision.

name: German Empire
story: The black-white-red banner proclaimed a German empire forged by 'blood and iron' in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles - an insult France repaid in 1919, in the same hall. Bismarck's creation was Europe's industrial colossus: chemical dyes, electrical engineering, the world's best universities, and a social-insurance system invented to outflank the socialists. Its undoing was the master's own prophecy - 'some damned foolish thing in the Balkans' - which came true at Sarajevo in 1914. Four years of trench war ended with the Kaiser fleeing to Holland, the empire dissolved, and Versailles drawing borders that lit the next war's fuse.
quizFact: Bismarck predicted 20 years in advance that 'some damned foolish thing in the Balkans' would start the next great war.

name: Austria-Hungary
story: The red-white-red and red-white-green civil ensign joined two crowns under one emperor, ruling 11 nationalities from Vienna. The empire began WWI over the Sarajevo assassination and dissolved overnight in 1918 into six new countries.
quizFact: There was no single joint flag for the two halves; the compromise ensign was only for merchant ships.

name: Russian Empire
story: The tsar's tricolour stretched across eleven time zones - the largest continuous state on Earth, built by fur traders, Cossacks and exiles. Peter the Great built St Petersburg on a swamp with 40,000 deaths and beat Sweden at Poltava; Catherine the Great took Crimea and Poland's shares; Romanovs reigned for 304 years over a realm where 80% could not read. The end was a collapse of bread and belief: February 1917 took the tsar, October took the state, and the family died in a Yekaterinburg basement - the empire's lands became the USSR within five years.
quizFact: Russia sold Alaska to the USA in 1867 for $7.2 million, about two cents an acre.

name: Soviet Union
story: The hammer and sickle flew over the state that turned medieval farms into the world's second superpower in one generation - and buried its failures in unmarked ground. Collectivization starved Ukraine's Holodomor (3.5 million dead), the Great Purge shot 700,000 in two years, and the Gulag held 18 million at its peak. The same state industrialized fast enough to break the Wehrmacht at Stalingrad, put Gagarin in orbit, and arm half the planet's revolutions. It fell not to invasion but to arithmetic: by 1991 the queues were longer than the missile range, and Gorbachev's openness dissolved what no army could.
quizFact: The flag was lowered over the Kremlin on Christmas Day 1991, ending the Cold War era.

name: Qing Dynasty
story: The yellow dragon banner flew over China's greatest territorial extent and its deepest humiliation. Manchu emperors Kangxi and Qianlong doubled the empire, erasing the Dzungar people in the process; the population reached 450 million. Then the Opium Wars forced treaty ports and the Taiping Rebellion killed 20-30 million - more than WWI - while Empress Dowager Cixi ruled behind screens for 47 years and spent navy money on a marble boat. The 1911 revolution ended 2,000 years of imperial rule; the last emperor, Puyi, was six years old and later died a gardener.
quizFact: The Qing forced every Han man to wear the Manchu queue braid on pain of death, a badge of conquest for 250 years.

name: Republic of China (Beiyang era)
file: Flag of the Republic of China (1912-1928).svg
story: The five-coloured flag of Han, Manchu, Mongol, Hui and Tibetan unity flew over China's first republic, born from the 1911 revolution. Warlords shredded it until the Nationalists' Northern Expedition replaced it with the blue-sky flag in 1928.
quizFact: Each stripe stood for one of China's five principal peoples, a flag designed to bind an empire into a nation.

name: Empire of Japan
story: The Rising Sun carried Japan from feudal isolation to the destruction of the Russian fleet at Tsushima in 1905 - the first modern defeat of a European power by an Asian nation - and then into the abyss. Korea was annexed in 1910, Manchuria seized in 1931, and the 1937 Nanjing massacre killed 200,000-300,000 in six weeks; Unit 731 tested plague on living prisoners. The army answered to no cabinet, and assassinated the ministers who tried to restrain it. The Pacific war ended only under two atomic clouds; the emperor who was worshipped as a god renounced divinity on radio, and the empire dissolved into a democracy that renounced war.
quizFact: The 1905 victory at Tsushima was the first time an Asian power beat a European great power in a modern war.

name: Kingdom of Siam
story: The white elephant on red flew over the one Southeast Asian kingdom that never fell to Europe. Kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernized fast and played the British and French off each other, keeping Siam independent.
quizFact: The elephant was removed from the flag after a king was gifted two unusual white elephants that were not 'perfect' enough for royal symbolism.

name: Korean Empire
story: The taegeuk flag flew over Korea's short-lived empire, declared in 1897 to assert independence between Japan, China and Russia. Japan annexed the peninsula in 1910, and the flag survived only in the independence movement, returning in 1945.
quizFact: The flag's design was drafted with help from a US diplomat in 1882 because Korea lacked a national flag for foreign talks.

name: Empire of Brazil
story: The green banner with the imperial crown flew over the only monarchy in the Americas, ruled by Dom Pedro I and II, son and grandson of Portugal's king. Generals declared a republic in 1889 after the abolition of slavery, and the emperor sailed into exile.
quizFact: Dom Pedro II was arguably the best-educated ruler of his day; he corresponded with scientists and skipped a world's fair to avoid a coup, which happened anyway.

name: Gran Colombia
story: The yellow-blue-red flag of Bolívar's dream: one great republic from Venezuela to Ecuador, forged in the wars against Spain. Bolívar's death in 1830 and regional rivalries split it into Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador within a year.
quizFact: Bolívar liberated four countries and died at 47, famously bitter: 'I have ploughed the sea'. His flag's colours live on in three national flags.

name: Confederate States ('Stars and Bars')
file: Flag of the Confederate States of America (1861-1863).svg
story: The first Confederate flag flew over the southern states that seceded to protect slavery, sparking the US Civil War. Four years of fighting ended at Appomattox in 1865, the Confederacy dissolved, and the Union was restored at a cost of 620,000 lives.
quizFact: The 'Stars and Bars' was replaced in 1863 because it looked too much like the Union's own flag on smoky battlefields.

name: Yugoslavia (Socialist)
story: The blue-white-red flag with a red star flew over Tito's federation of six republics, held together by one leader and one party. Tito died in 1980, nationalism rose through the decade, and the country shattered in the Yugoslav Wars of the 1990s.
quizFact: 'Yugoslavia' simply means 'land of the South Slavs', and Tito's non-aligned bloc annoyed both Washington and Moscow.

name: East Germany (DDR)
story: The tricolour with hammer and compass flew over the Soviet-built German state, walled into Berlin in 1961. When Hungary opened its borders in 1989 and the Wall fell that November, East Germany dissolved into reunified Germany by October 1990.
quizFact: East Germany's Stasi employed one informant for every 6.5 citizens, one of the highest surveillance ratios ever.

name: Rhodesia
story: The green-white flag flew over a white-minority state that declared independence from Britain in 1965 to avoid majority rule. Guerrilla war brought it down: in 1979-80 it became Zimbabwe under Robert Mugabe.
quizFact: Rhodesia's UDI (Unilateral Declaration of Independence) was the first such break by a British colony since 1776.

name: Tibet (1912–1951)
story: The snow lion flag flew over Tibet's de facto independence between the fall of the Qing and the People's Republic. Chinese troops entered in 1950, the 17-point agreement of 1951 absorbed Tibet, and the Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959.
quizFact: The flag design pairs two snow lions holding a yin-yang flame jewel, and it is still banned in China.

name: Kingdom of Hawaii
story: King Kamehameha I united the islands and adopted this flag with Union Jack stripes and eight bars for the eight main islands. American sugar planters and marines overthrew Queen Liliuokalani in 1893, and the US annexed Hawaii in 1898.
quizFact: Hawaii's state flag today is still the kingdom's flag, the only US state flag to feature another country's flag.

name: Ethiopian Empire
story: The green-yellow-red tricolour flew over the one African nation that beat a European colonizer, crushing Italy at Adwa in 1896. Haile Selassie ruled until the 1974 famine and Marxist coup deposed him, ending a 700-year monarchy.
quizFact: Adwa's victory made Ethiopia a symbol of African independence; many new African flags borrowed its colours.

name: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
story: The white eagle and knight banner flew over Europe's largest and most tolerant state, where kings were elected and nobles had veto power. Russia, Prussia and Austria devoured it in three partitions (1772, 1793, 1795), erasing it from the map for 123 years.
quizFact: The Commonwealth elected its kings, and any noble could veto parliament with a single 'Liberum veto' — a flaw its neighbours exploited.

name: Republic of Venice
file: Flag of the Republic of Venice.svg
story: The winged Lion of St Mark flew over a merchant republic of a thousand years, ruling the seas from the Adriatic to Crete. Napoleon's armies ended it in 1797, handing the ancient city to Austria, and the lion's legend lives on Venice's flag today.
quizFact: Venice ran the Mediterranean's banks, glass (Murano) and silk trades, and its Doges ruled for 1,100 years without a single dynasty.

name: Kingdom of Jerusalem
file: Arms of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.svg
story: The gold cross on white flew over the crusader state founded after the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099. Saladin retook the city in 1187, and the last crusader fortress at Acre fell in 1291, ending two centuries of Outremer.
quizFact: Saladin and Richard the Lionheart never met in person, though they negotiated prisoner exchanges by messenger.

name: Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen
file: Flag of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen.svg
story: The five-pointed red star banner flew over Yemen's Zaydi imams after the Ottoman collapse. Nasser-inspired officers overthrew the kingdom in the 1962 coup, starting a civil war that drew in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.
quizFact: Yemeni imams once ruled from mountain fortress-cities with flags signalling royal decrees to the valleys.

name: Kingdom of Egypt
story: The green banner with crescent and three stars flew over a nominally independent kingdom under King Fuad and Farouk, still shadowed by Britain. Free Officers led by Nasser toppled Farouk in 1952, and the republic's eagle replaced the crown.
quizFact: The three stars stood for Egypt, Sudan and Nubia; the revolution's green banner was replaced within a year.

name: Qajar Iran
story: The Lion and Sun over red flew at first under the Qajar shahs, who lost the Caucasus to Russia and conceded oil to the British. The 1921 coup put Reza Khan on the throne, ending the dynasty and founding Pahlavi Iran.
quizFact: The Lion and Sun emblem appeared on Iranian flags for over 500 years, surviving every dynasty until 1979.

name: Kingdom of Sikkim
story: The khyang-phro flag with the Buddhist wheel flew over a Namgyal dynasty in the Himalayas for 333 years. Referendum and unrest led India to absorb Sikkim as a state in 1975, ending the monarchy.
quizFact: Sikkim was the last Indian princely state to join the union, and its Chogyal kings claimed descent from Indra's line.

name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
file: Flag of the Sultanate of Zanzibar.svg
story: The red flag of the Omani sultans flew over the clove island capital of the Indian Ocean trade. The 1964 revolution overthrew the last sultan, and Zanzibar merged with Tanganyika months later to form Tanzania.
quizFact: Zanzibar was once the world's largest clove producer, and its sultans kept a resident consort of princes from Muscat.

name: Tsardom of Russia
story: Ivan the Terrible crowned himself first Tsar, and the Romanovs began in 1613 a line that would stretch to Siberia and the Pacific. Peter the Great modernized the state and crowned himself Emperor in 1721, renaming it an empire.
quizFact: Peter the Great taxed beards, forcing noblemen who refused to shave to carry a copper 'beard token'.

name: Kalmar Union
story: Margaret I of Denmark united Norway, Sweden and Denmark under one crown at Kalmar, the largest realm in Europe at the time. Swedish resistance under Gustav Vasa broke the union in 1523, founding Sweden's independence.
quizFact: Margaret ruled through adopted heirs and wardship, a queen with no formal title over three kingdoms.

name: Aztec (Triple Alliance)
story: No surviving Aztec flag exists; the eagle-on-cactus emblem that Cortés saw as a prophecy became Mexico's own. The Mexica built Tenochtitlan on a lake, ruled Mesoamerica through tribute, and fell to Cortés, smallpox and native allies in 1521.
quizFact: The Mexican flag's eagle scene is based on an Aztec founding myth that Cortés recorded hearing in 1519.

name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)
story: The rainbow banner associated with the Incas is a modern Cusco invention, but the empire it represents was real: 40,000 km of roads, quipu records and 12 million people from Ecuador to Chile. Pizarro's 1532 ambush at Cajamarca ended it in a single afternoon.
quizFact: Cusco's rainbow flag was adopted in 1978; the Incas themselves kept records in knotted strings instead of flags or writing.

name: Nazi Germany (Third Reich)
story: The swastika flag flew over the dictatorship that started WWII in Europe and murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust, alongside Roma, disabled people, Slavs and political prisoners. Hitler's empire swallowed Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland and France by 1940, promising a 'thousand years' and lasting twelve. It ended in Berlin's rubble in May 1945; the flag is banned in Germany and many other countries today.
quizFact: Under the Nuremberg Laws of 1935, the swastika flag became Germany's only national flag - one of the first legal steps toward the Holocaust.

name: Kingdom of Italy
story: The Savoy tricolour with a shield flew over the unified Italy that Cavour and Garibaldi stitched together from seven states, over the colonial disasters in Ethiopia (Adwa, 1896 - the first time a European power lost to Africa), both world wars, and Mussolini's two decades of fascism. Italians voted the monarchy away by referendum in 1946 by two million votes - the royal house went into exile and the plain tricolour replaced it.
quizFact: The Savoy coat of arms on the flag's centre was cross out on official photos after the 1946 referendum - the vote that abolished the kingdom.

name: Teutonic Order
story: A crusading order of German knight-monks in black crosses, invited to the Baltic to convert pagans and staying to build a military state. They ruled Prussia and Livonia from castles like Marienburg, fought Poland and Lithuania for 200 years, and were broken at Grunwald/Tannenberg in 1410 - one of medieval Europe's largest battles. The order secularized in 1525 when its Grand Master converted to Lutheranism and made Prussia a duchy.
quizFact: The order's state, not its faith, survived it: its Prussian heartland became the duchy that later unified Germany.

name: Papal States
story: For over a thousand years the Popes ruled central Italy as princes - crowning emperors, excommunicating kings, and fielding armies. The States were founded on the forged 'Donation of Constantine' and ended when Italian reunification took Rome in 1870; the Pope shut himself in the Vatican as a self-declared 'prisoner' until the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created the Vatican City state that remains today.
quizFact: The Papal States' army included the Swiss Guard - founded in 1506, and still guarding the Pope today as the world's smallest army.

name: Republic of Genoa
file: Flag of the Republic of Genoa.svg
story: Genoa the Proud ruled Mediterranean banking and shipping for 700 years, bankrolling Spain's American ventures and minting admirals like Columbus - a Genoese who sailed for Spain because Genoa would not fund him. It fought Venice to exhaustion in four wars, then faded as Atlantic trade passed it by. Napoleon - born a Genoese subject in Corsica the year after France bought the island - abolished the republic in 1797.
quizFact: Genoa's red-and-white banner is the origin of England's St George's Cross - the English adopted it from Genoese ships to protect their vessels.

name: Dutch Republic (Prince's Flag)
story: The orange-white-blue Prince's Flag flew over the Dutch Revolt against Spain - the 'Sea Beggars' who flooded their own land to drown a Spanish army - and over the founding of the VOC, the richest company in history. It was replaced by the plain red-white-blue tricolour in 1630, but echoes survive: New Amsterdam (New York) was founded under it, and its orange band is remembered in the Dutch royal house's colour to this day.
quizFact: The Prince's Flag is considered the first tricolour in the modern sense - the model for Russia's and France's flags.

name: South Africa (Union)
story: The 'Oranje-Banje-Blauw' flew over South Africa from the reconciliation of Boer and Brit after their war, through apartheid's creation in 1948, to its dismantling in 1994. Three flags in one - Union Jack, Orange Free State Vierkleur and Transvaal Krusvlag - it represented a state built on white minority rule. It came down when Nelson Mandela's government adopted the new rainbow flag after the first democratic elections.
quizFact: The old flag contained two other flags inside it - a rare 'flag within a flag within a flag' design.

name: Congo Free State
file: Flag of the Congo Free State.svg
story: A yellow star on blue flew over King Leopold II's private empire - 76 times the size of Belgium, owned personally by one man. The rubber regime took hostages, cut hands for missed quotas, and killed or worked to death an estimated 1 to 15 million people. The first global human-rights photo campaign, led by missionaries and Roger Casement's report, forced Belgium to take the colony from its own king in 1908.
quizFact: The star on the modern Congolese flag is the same star that flew over Leopold's rubber regime - kept as a symbol of independence hope.

name: Mongolia (Bogd Khanate)
story: When the Qing dynasty collapsed in 1911, Outer Mongolia declared independence under the Eighth Jebtsundamba - the Bogd Khan, a reincarnated lama who was both head of religion and state. The soyombo symbol flew over a theocratic kingdom squeezed between newly republican China and revolutionary Russia. In 1921 the Red Army and Mongolian revolutionaries took the capital; the Bogd Khan died two years later and the monarchy was abolished, ending a reincarnation line that had chosen its leaders for 350 years.
quizFact: The Bogd Khan was simultaneously a reincarnated god, a king, and - reportedly - a collector of cars and circus dwarfs.

name: Orange Free State
file: Flag of the Orange Free State.svg
story: The Voortrekkers who fled British rule in the Cape founded an orange-and-white republic on the high veld, modelled on the USA's constitution. It fought Britain twice - the second time alongside the Transvaal in the Boer War, where British scorched-earth tactics and concentration camps killed 26,000 civilians. It lost in 1902 and became part of the Union of South Africa in 1910.
quizFact: The flag's orange bars were said to represent the Orange River's banks - designed by a Dutch princess-in-exile, the future Queen Wilhelmina's tutor.

name: South African Republic (Transvaal)
story: The 'Vierkleur' - four colours - flew over the Boer republic that struck the world's richest gold at Witwatersrand in 1886. Within 15 years the gold had drawn British imperial attention: the failed Jameson Raid of 1895, then the Boer War. Under President Paul Kruger the Vierkleur resisted the empire until 1902; the Union Jack replaced it, and apartheid's designers later invoked the old republic's memory.
quizFact: The Vierkleur was the flag carried at the Boer War's battles - and one was taken to the Moon's vicinity aboard Apollo by a South African astronaut candidate.

name: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
file: Flag of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.svg
story: The largest of Italy's pre-unification states - Naples and Sicily under a Bourbon king - with the peninsula's first railway and steamship lines. Garibaldi's thousand redshirts landed in 1860 and toppled it in five months; the kingdom joined unified Italy by plebiscite. Its treasury, meant to fund the new Italy, was spent on crushing the south's 'brigand' resistance instead.
quizFact: The Two Sicilies had Italy's first steamship line - and its real estate spanned from Rome's door to Greece's doorstep.

name: Crusader States (Outremer)
file: Flag of the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099-1291).svg
story: The cross potent between four crosslets marked two centuries of European crusader kingdoms on the Levantine coast, from the mass capture of Jerusalem in 1099 to the last fortress at Acre in 1291. Founded by war and pilgrimage, they built castles like Krak des Chevaliers that still stand. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187; the Mamluks swept the rest, and the sea took the survivors home.
quizFact: The Kingdom of Jerusalem's royal title passed to the kings of Cyprus and later to the kings of Naples - who held it for 500 years after the kingdom itself was gone.

name: Kingdom of Hungary (Medieval)
story: Stephen I took a crown from the Pope in 1000 and turned Magyar raiders into a Christian kingdom that checked Mongols at the Danube and rivaled Austria. Matthias Corvinus' black army of mercenaries was Europe's finest in the 1400s, and his library the largest north of the Alps. The kingdom shattered at Mohacs in 1526 against Suleiman's cannons - a defeat Hungarians still mourn as their greatest.
quizFact: Matthias Corvinus' 'Black Army' was Europe's first professional standing mercenary force - paid, uniformed, and feared from Vienna to the Balkans.

name: Duchy of Burgundy
file: Flag of the Valois Dukes of Burgundy.svg
story: The Valois dukes of Burgundy were richer and more cultivated than their French kings - patrons of van Eyck, masters of Flanders' cloth trade, dreamers of a kingdom from the North Sea to the Alps. Charles the Bold nearly built it, dying in 1477 frozen in a swamp at Nancy against the Swiss pikemen; his heiress Mary married the Habsburg Maximilian, and her dowry - the Low Countries - became the seed of the Spanish and Austrian empires. The duchy itself was swallowed by France.
quizFact: The 'Order of the Golden Fleece', founded by Burgundy in 1430, is still Europe's most exclusive chivalric order - now split between Spain and Austria.

name: Republic of Florence
story: The city of the lily minted the florin - the dollar of the Middle Ages - and bred the Renaissance: Dante, Giotto, Leonardo, Michelangelo and Machiavelli all lived under its banner. The Medici bankers ruled from behind the curtains, survived a papal assassination plot (the Pazzi conspiracy, 1478), and finally made themselves dukes. Charles V's armies ended the republic in 1532.
quizFact: Florence's florin was so reliable it was used unchanged for 300 years - the medieval world's reserve currency.

name: Khedivate of Egypt
story: The semi-independent Egypt of the Khedives built Cairo's opera house (for Aida), the Suez Canal, and a sugar economy - then bankrupted itself funding both canal and conquest, selling the canal's shares to Britain in 1875. British troops occupied in 1882 'to protect investments' and stayed 70 years. The flag's crescents and star flew over a state that was sovereign on paper and pawned in fact - the pattern Egypt's 1952 revolution rose against.
quizFact: When Egypt sold its Suez Canal shares in 1875, Britain bought them in 11 days - the world's fastest multi-million-pound deal, done by telegraph.

name: Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen (flag detail)
file: Flag of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen.svg
story: The five-pointed red star banner flew over Yemen's Zaydi imams, who ruled mountain fortresses while the Ottomans and later the British circled the coasts. Imam Yahya was assassinated in 1948 in a palace coup that failed; his son Ahmed kept the medieval throne running on a radio address that told citizens 'obey me'. Nasser-inspired officers finally toppled the kingdom in 1962, starting a civil war that became Egypt and Saudi Arabia's proxy battleground.
quizFact: Imam Yahya ruled with a tradition that no foreign map of Yemen could be published - geography itself was a state secret.

name: First Mexican Empire
file: Flag of the First Mexican Empire.svg
story: Mexico's independence came not from a revolution won but from a bargain made: royalist officer Agustin de Iturbide switched sides, marched with the rebels into Mexico City, and was crowned Emperor Agustin I over an empire stretching from Oregon to Panama - the largest North American empire since Spain's. He ruled less than a year; debts and temper lost the army's loyalty, he abdicated in 1823, and when he returned in 1824 he was shot. Central America broke away the same year.
quizFact: Iturbide's empire was so vast that at its founding ceremony the crowned eagle flag was blessed with the title 'Monarchia Mexicana'.

name: Sikh Empire (Punjab)
story: Maharaja Ranjit Singh - one-eyed from smallpox, illiterate, called the 'Lion of Punjab' - forged the last major state to resist British conquest of India, ruling from Lahore over 350,000 km2. His Khalsa army included Sikh, Muslim and Hindu generals and even European mercenaries. He died in 1839; four assassinations and two child-kings later, the British invaded, won the two Anglo-Sikh Wars, and exiled the boy maharaja Duleep Singh to England - where he became Queen Victoria's friend and died penniless.
quizFact: Ranjit Singh's empire was the last independent Indian state to fall to the British - and the Koh-i-Noor diamond came from his treasury.

name: Kingdom of Mysore
file: Flag of the Kingdom of Mysore.svg
story: Under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan - the 'Tiger of Mysore' - Mysore built rocket artillery that stunned British armies and came within a treaty of expelling them from India. Tipu was killed defending his capital in 1799, his mechanical tiger mauling a British soldier now in a London museum. The Wodeyar dynasty was restored under British 'guidance' and ruled as a model princely state until 1950.
quizFact: Tipu Sultan's iron-cased rockets were reverse-engineered by the British and inspired the Congreve rockets used at Waterloo.

name: Fatimid Caliphate
story: The Ismaili Fatimids claimed descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima and carved an empire from Tunisia to Egypt and Syria, founding Cairo in 969 and al-Azhar - today the world's oldest running university. Their navy ruled the eastern Mediterranean; their caliph al-Hakim was so erratic he outlawed molokhia and, legend says, walked into the hills one night and vanished. Power slipped to viziers, Saladin took over in 1171, and the green banners fell.
quizFact: Cairo was founded by the Fatimids as a new capital named 'the Victorious' - after the planet Mars, al-Qahira, was 'in the ascendant' that night.

name: Ayyubid Sultanate
story: Saladin - Kurdish by birth - ended the Fatimid caliphate and united Egypt and Syria, then took Jerusalem back from the Crusaders in 1187 after the Battle of Hattin. Even his enemies praised his chivalry: he ransomed rather than massacred the city's Christians, and traded gifts with Richard the Lionheart without ever meeting him. The dynasty withered into rival principalities and was replaced by its own Mamluk bodyguards in 1250 - who then stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut.
quizFact: Saladin's bodyguard included a Mamluk corps that later outlived and replaced his whole dynasty.
